## The short version

Machine learning is not new to atmospheric science. Statistical post-processing, analog methods, neural networks, automated retrievals, downscaling, pattern recognition, and empirical parameterizations all have long histories in the field. Many researchers have used the label *machine learning* only recently for ideas that climate science has developed in other vocabularies for decades.

Recent data-driven weather models are nonetheless a substantial technical development. They have brought new architectures, unusually large training datasets, rapid inference, and fresh attention to the possibility of learning parts of the Earth-system modeling workflow. But they are neither the beginning of machine learning in atmospheric science nor evidence that physical climate modeling has been superseded.

Weather prediction asks how a known atmospheric state will evolve over days. Climate science often asks how the coupled Earth system responds to forcing it has not previously experienced, how its statistics change over decades, and why. A model can excel at interpolation within the historical record while being unreliable under a changed climate. It can reproduce a forecast metric without representing the process that gives the metric scientific meaning.

The useful question in 2026 is not whether AI has "changed everything." It is where modern machine learning adds capabilities that are genuinely useful for climate science, and where familiar problems—sampling, nonstationarity, physical consistency, uncertainty, and interpretation—remain. The demanding tests are whether learned components remain stable when coupled, preserve distributions and budgets, respond credibly outside the training climate, quantify uncertainty, and help discriminate among scientific explanations.

The field is advancing along several distinct paths: learned forecast models; data-driven and hybrid climate simulators; parameterizations trained from high-resolution simulations; fast emulators of expensive models; generative downscaling; machine learning for observations and data assimilation; probabilistic models of extremes; and methods intended to extract physical relationships rather than only make predictions. These paths share tools, but they do not share the same standard of success.

The central claim of this first issue is simple:

> The relevant question is not whether a model is called AI, but whether it participates reliably in scientific inference.

That transition has begun, but it is incomplete.

## Weather forecasting is a useful reference point, not the origin story

Recent AI weather models have received more attention than most earlier uses of ML in atmospheric science. Graph neural networks, transformers, neural operators, and generative models have demonstrated that fast, data-driven global forecasts can be competitive with numerical weather prediction on many standard measures. This is important progress, but it should not be mistaken for a scientific rupture.

The progression matters. Early headline results centered on deterministic medium-range forecasts. NeuralGCM then showed that a hybrid model—a differentiable dynamical core combined with learned components—could support deterministic forecasts, ensembles, and multi-decadal atmosphere-only simulations [@kochkov2024neuralgcm]. GenCast made probabilistic forecasting central rather than optional, using a diffusion model to generate ensembles of plausible 15-day trajectories [@price2025gencast]. Aardvark pushed farther upstream by learning a path from raw observations to global and local forecasts, reducing its dependence on a conventional numerical analysis at deployment time [@allen2025aardvark]. Aurora broadened the ambition from one forecasting task to a pretrained Earth-system model that could be adapted across atmospheric and environmental applications [@bodnar2025aurora].

They matter to climate research for three specific reasons.

First, they prove that useful global geophysical models can be dramatically cheaper to run. That changes the feasible size of ensembles, the speed of sensitivity experiments, and access to sophisticated prediction tools.

Second, they provide architectures and training strategies that can be adapted to seasonal prediction, model emulation, downscaling, data assimilation, and coupled simulation.

Third, they have forced a productive reconsideration of which parts of the traditional pipeline are indispensable. If the forecast model can be learned, can the observation operator, assimilation system, parameterizations, or coupled components be learned as well?

But the weather results should not be overgeneralized. Most leading systems learn from reanalysis, which is not raw nature but a physically structured synthesis of observations and numerical modeling. Forecast skill over days does not establish a correct response to rising carbon dioxide. Stable rollouts do not by themselves establish correct climate statistics. And a lower average error can coexist with weaknesses in rare events, spatial structure, conservation, or ensemble calibration.

Weather forecasting is therefore a useful reference point for current capabilities and limits. It is not the origin story of ML in atmospheric science, nor the template against which every climate application should be judged.

## From learned forecasts to learned climate simulators

A climate simulator must do more than remain numerically alive for a long time. It must produce credible equilibria, forced responses, internal variability, teleconnections, extremes, and interactions among the atmosphere, ocean, land, cryosphere, and biogeochemistry.

There are two broad strategies. Fully data-driven models learn nearly the entire state transition. Hybrid models retain an explicit numerical core or physical components and use machine learning where conventional formulations are expensive, uncertain, or incomplete.

NeuralGCM is an important hybrid example because its long integrations reproduced multiple atmospheric climate statistics while retaining resolved dynamics [@kochkov2024neuralgcm]. Its limitation is equally instructive: the reported model did not extrapolate to substantially different future climates. That is not a footnote. It marks the difference between reproducing a historical attractor and predicting a forced response. Work coupling ACE2 to a slab ocean takes a more direct step toward the latter question, evaluating equilibrium and transient responses across changed CO2 concentrations [@clark2025ace2som].

Work on coupled emulators is beginning to expose the next layer of difficulty. Samudra has shown that a learned global ocean emulator can reproduce vertical structure and interannual variability without drift over its evaluated period [@dheeshjith2025samudra]. SamudrACE then couples learned atmosphere and three-dimensional ocean components and can produce centuries-long simulations with atmosphere, ocean, sea ice, and surface variables [@duncan2025samudrace]. Results of this kind are scientifically interesting because coupled variability—ENSO is the obvious test—cannot be recovered by treating sea-surface temperatures as prescribed boundary conditions.

Yet even a coupled emulator generally learns a reference model, not the Earth directly. Its speed can enable experiments that the parent simulator makes impractical, but it may also inherit the parent's structural errors and cannot automatically be trusted in forcing regimes absent from training. The honest description is often *emulator of a model climate*, not replacement for a climate model or discovery of the climate system.

The most convincing future evaluations will therefore resemble climate-model evaluation rather than weather leaderboards. They will test responses across forcing levels, energy and water budgets, modes of variability, feedbacks, extremes, and out-of-distribution climates. They will also compare against simple baselines and ask whether the learned system contributes information beyond efficiently reproducing its training simulator.

## Parameterizations are becoming a coupled-learning problem

Subgrid parameterization may be the area where machine learning most directly confronts a longstanding scientific limitation. Clouds, convection, turbulence, ocean mixing, radiation, and land processes operate below the resolved grid yet influence circulation and climate sensitivity. High-resolution simulations can provide training targets that conventional parameterizations struggle to encode.

The early version of this idea sounded straightforward: run an expensive cloud-resolving model, coarse-grain its output, train a neural network to predict tendencies, and insert the network into a global model. In practice, a parameterization with excellent offline scores can destabilize its host model. Small errors alter the resolved state, which moves the model away from the training distribution, which produces larger errors. The parameterization and the circulation form a coupled dynamical system; evaluating one as a static regression misses the main problem.

Recent work is increasingly designed around this reality. Experience-replay training has produced multi-year stable simulations when a learned physics package was coupled to the Community Atmosphere Model [@chen2025experience]. A decadal hybrid simulation with learned cloud and convection physics has also demonstrated stability in a warmer climate, with results emphasizing the value of process memory, richer inputs, and training choices designed for online behavior [@han2025warmclimate]. ClimSim and its associated competition helped make the offline problem reproducible, but the more consequential result is that multiple competition-derived architectures could subsequently run stably online—while no single model dominated every metric [@lin2026climsim].

This changes how progress should be measured. Architecture novelty matters less than:

- stability after coupling;
- fidelity of the simulated climate rather than one-step tendencies;
- behavior under warming or transfer to another host model;
- conservation and physically meaningful constraints;
- stochastic variability rather than regression to a conditional mean;
- computational performance inside the actual simulator.

Machine-learning parameterizations are not merely faster curve fits. At their best, they are a way to connect high-resolution process knowledge to global climate dynamics. But the scientific object is the coupled model, not the neural network in isolation.

## Emulation changes which experiments are possible

Full Earth-system simulations are expensive enough that climate science routinely works with sparse ensembles, a limited set of scenarios, and imperfect sampling of internal variability. Emulators learn mappings from forcings, parameters, or model states to outputs of interest. They can range from simple statistical response surfaces to autoregressive global field models.

Their immediate value is computational. A sufficiently faithful emulator can fill gaps between expensive simulations, generate large ensembles, accelerate uncertainty quantification, support parameter calibration, or make interactive exploration possible. The more important consequence is experimental: questions that were previously too costly can become routine.

This is why the emerging proposal to co-design simulators and emulators is more compelling than treating emulation as post-processing [@vankatwyk2026emulators]. Existing atmospheric emulators already illustrate the possible gain: ACE has been applied to E3SM's atmosphere with attention to precipitation fidelity, while LUCIE evaluated long integrations and large ensembles with explicit physical-consistency diagnostics [@duncan2024ace; @guan2025lucie]. A future modeling campaign could choose expensive simulations partly for the information they add to an emulator, use uncertainty estimates to identify where new simulations are needed, and provide standardized data and benchmarks for downstream analysis.

But an emulator's epistemic status should remain explicit. It can interpolate a simulator very accurately and still tell us nothing new about whether that simulator is right. It can generate a dense ensemble whose apparent precision hides sparse training support. And speed does not repair structural uncertainty. This is not merely hypothetical: a recent benchmark analysis found that simple pattern scaling could outperform a much larger learned emulator for some regional variables once internal variability was handled carefully [@lutjens2025benchmark].

The strongest use is therefore often a partnership: the simulator supplies physically coherent counterfactual experiments; the emulator expands their coverage; observations constrain both; and uncertainty determines where further computation is valuable.

## Downscaling is moving from one answer to a distribution

Regional climate information is both scientifically difficult and societally important. Coarse global models do not resolve local terrain, convection, and many extremes. Traditional statistical downscaling can be efficient but often smooths variability or relies on stationarity assumptions. Dynamical downscaling retains more physics but is computationally expensive.

Generative machine learning reframes the problem. A coarse state does not determine one unique fine-scale state, so a downscaler should often estimate a conditional distribution rather than a single high-resolution image. Diffusion models, flows, and other stochastic approaches can generate multiple locally detailed realizations consistent with the large-scale conditions.

Recent methods have demonstrated scale-adaptive, uncertainty-aware generation of high-resolution Earth-system fields [@hess2025downscaling]. EnScale extends this direction to temporally consistent, multivariate generative downscaling, including an evaluation of heavy-rainfall behavior [@schillinger2026enscale]. The advance is not simply sharper-looking maps. It is the possibility of representing unresolved variability and producing ensembles at a cost compatible with risk analysis.

The caution is that visual realism is a weak validation criterion. A useful climate downscaler must preserve temporal coherence, multivariate relationships, spatial dependence, extremes, and responses to climate change. It must also separate uncertainty inherited from the global model from uncertainty introduced by the downscaling method. A generated storm texture can look convincing while having the wrong frequency, persistence, or thermodynamic scaling.

Downscaling is therefore one of the clearest places where proper probabilistic evaluation—not image quality—will determine whether generative AI becomes scientifically useful.

## Observations and data assimilation may be the quieter revolution

Climate knowledge depends on incomplete, heterogeneous observations. Satellites change, stations move, retrieval algorithms introduce assumptions, and many variables are only indirectly observed. Machine learning is already used for retrievals, gap filling, reconstruction, quality control, bias correction, and extracting structure from high-dimensional Earth observations [@bracco2025physics]. Recent deep-learning reconstruction of Antarctic surface temperatures provides one concrete example, and makes clear why independent validation against withheld observations remains essential [@wang2025antarctic].

The convergence with data assimilation is particularly important. Data assimilation combines observations, a forecast model, and uncertainty to estimate the evolving state of the Earth system. Machine learning can emulate expensive observation operators, learn model error, estimate covariance structure, accelerate inference, or approximate parts of the assimilation cycle. Conversely, data assimilation offers machinery for constraining learned models with observations and propagating uncertainty [@arcucci2026assimilation]. Proof-of-concept work has used ML to accelerate high-resolution observation handling [@howard2024assimilation], while recent coupled-model work uses assimilation increments to learn systematic ocean-model error [@verma2026oceanerror].

This area complicates claims of a clean replacement of physics by data. Many successful AI models are trained on reanalysis and therefore inherit the products of data assimilation and numerical modeling. End-to-end forecasting systems make the dependency more visible by attempting to learn state estimation and forecasting together, but they do not eliminate the need to reason about observational error, sampling, and physical consistency.

For climate, the prize is larger than a better initial condition. Better integration of observations and models could improve reanalysis, extend records, identify model-error patterns, and provide more direct constraints on forced responses. The risk is that learned reconstructions make uncertain or missing information look complete. Traceable uncertainty will matter as much as spatial coverage.

## Extremes make probability unavoidable

Climate risk is often controlled by distribution tails, spatial dependence, and compound events rather than mean conditions. This exposes the weakness of deterministic models optimized for average error. A prediction close to the conditional mean can score well while suppressing the very extremes that matter.

Generative weather models such as GenCast demonstrate that learned ensembles can represent multiple plausible trajectories rather than a single smoothed future [@price2025gencast]. Similar ideas are entering downscaling, event generation, tropical-cyclone modeling, and estimates of precipitation and heat extremes. At regional scale, AI systems are also being evaluated directly for atmospheric rivers and extreme precipitation rather than only average forecast error [@pan2025regionalai].

The scientific challenge is data scarcity. The rarest events are, by definition, poorly sampled. Historical observations are short relative to many return periods, and the distribution itself changes with forcing. A flexible generative model can reproduce or amplify patterns without learning the correct causal response to warming.

Evaluation must therefore connect distributional skill to process. Does the model reproduce known thermodynamic scaling? Are compound dependencies credible? Are ensemble probabilities calibrated in held-out periods and regions? Do tail changes persist under alternative data sources and model configurations? Can the system express that it does not know?

For extremes, uncertainty quantification is not a decorative addition. It is the product.

## Prediction is not yet scientific understanding

The most important opportunity is also the easiest to oversell: using machine learning to learn about the climate system.

High-capacity models can detect regimes, compress complex fields, identify precursors, estimate nonlinear relationships, and rank influential variables. Interpretable models and causal methods can help generate hypotheses. Process-based machine learning can combine flexible estimation with relationships chosen for scientific meaning. For example, observationally trained relationships have been used to constrain regional warming projections, with an explicit focus on process-informed transfer rather than raw pattern matching [@wilkinson2025constraints]. Causal discovery has also been applied to high-dimensional space-time climate data, including a study of the atmospheric response to the Pinatubo eruption [@nichol2025castle].

But predictive association is not mechanism. Feature importance is not causality. A latent representation that separates regimes does not necessarily reveal why those regimes exist. And a neural network can exploit physically irrelevant correlations that are stable within one dataset. Causally informed parameterization work is promising precisely because it tests whether a reduced set of causal drivers transfers more robustly across climate states [@iglesiassuarez2024causal]. Interpretable model-error discovery from assimilation increments offers a complementary path from statistical correction to candidate equations [@mojgani2024medida].

Machine learning contributes to discovery when it is embedded in a chain of evidence:

1. a model identifies a reproducible pattern or candidate relationship;
2. the relationship survives changes in dataset, model, period, and climate regime;
3. physical reasoning turns it into a testable hypothesis;
4. targeted observations or controlled simulations challenge that hypothesis;
5. the result changes an explanation, parameterization, or prediction in a traceable way.

This standard is more demanding than benchmark improvement, but it is also where AI could have its largest scientific impact. Climate datasets are too large and nonlinear to inspect exhaustively, while climate theory alone cannot specify every useful representation. The productive role for machine learning is to help navigate the space between data and mechanism.

## The unresolved questions

Across these applications, a common set of problems determines whether progress is scientific or mainly computational.

### Generalization and nonstationarity

Future climates are outside the historical training distribution. Even training on climate-model scenarios does not guarantee transfer to the real forced response. Recent warm-climate parameterization experiments and CO2-perturbation emulator studies show both why this test is essential and how much more demanding it is than interpolation within a reference climate [@han2025warmclimate; @clark2025ace2som]. Tests across models, forcing levels, paleoclimates, abrupt-change experiments, and withheld regions are more informative than random train-test splits.

### Physical consistency

Exact conservation is not required of every diagnostic tool, but simulators and coupled components cannot accumulate small budget errors indefinitely. Long-term emulator studies now assess physical-consistency diagnostics explicitly, while stable learned parameterizations show that online behavior can differ fundamentally from one-step offline skill [@guan2025lucie; @chen2025experience]. Constraints should be evaluated for what they guarantee and what they merely encourage statistically.

### Long-term stability and climate fidelity

A stable model can have the wrong attractor. The distinction is visible in current long-integration studies of learned atmosphere and ocean emulators, which separately evaluate drift, mean state, variability, and extremes [@kochkov2024neuralgcm; @dheeshjith2025samudra; @guan2025lucie]. Long rollouts should be evaluated for mean state, variability, teleconnections, feedbacks, extremes, drift, and response—not only the absence of numerical failure.

### Uncertainty

Fast deterministic inference is less valuable if it conceals initial-condition, parameter, scenario, structural, and emulator uncertainty. Generative weather forecasting and downscaling studies make a useful distinction between generating conditional variability and establishing that the resulting probabilities are calibrated [@price2025gencast; @hess2025downscaling; @schillinger2026enscale]. Different uncertainties require different ensembles and should not be collapsed into one confidence score.

### Interpretability and causality

Post-hoc explanations can describe model sensitivity without identifying a physical cause. Recent space-time causal discovery and causally informed parameterization studies make their assumptions and validation settings explicit rather than treating an explanatory plot as causal evidence [@nichol2025castle; @iglesiassuarez2024causal]. Causal claims require assumptions, interventions, or natural experiments that make the identification strategy explicit.

### Benchmarks and scientific value

A benchmark rewards what it measures. Internal variability can even reverse apparent emulator rankings, and the first rounds of online parameterization evaluation show that no single architecture wins on every meaningful metric [@lutjens2025benchmark; @lin2026climsim]. Climate-relevant benchmarks must include distributional structure, conservation, regime shifts, coupled behavior, extremes, and out-of-distribution response. They should also ask whether a more complex model improves scientific decisions relative to a simpler baseline.

### Infrastructure and reproducibility

Large training datasets and expensive models can concentrate research capacity. The ClimSim competition and recent emulator perspectives illustrate the value of shared data, online evaluation, standardized benchmarks, and software designed around reproducibility [@lin2026climsim; @vankatwyk2026emulators]. Open evaluation data, documented preprocessing, reproducible baselines, and accessible pretrained models are not secondary concerns; they shape which claims the community can independently test.

## Where the field stands

In 2026, it is no longer credible to dismiss AI in climate science as a collection of toy demonstrations. Learned global forecasts work. Hybrid climate integrations can remain stable for years. Generative methods can represent unresolved regional variability. Coupled emulators are beginning to reproduce internally generated climate modes. Machine learning is entering data assimilation and process-based inference.

It is equally premature to describe this as a wholesale replacement of physical climate modeling. The strongest systems remain dependent on reanalysis, high-resolution simulation, conventional model output, physical cores, or combinations of all four. Their hardest tests—changed forcing, rare extremes, coupled feedbacks, uncertainty, and causal interpretation—are precisely the tests most important for climate science.

The likely future is not a contest with one winner. It is a modeling ecosystem in which numerical simulators, learned components, emulators, observations, and theory play different roles. The important research question is not whether a model is labeled *AI* or *physics-based*. It is what information went into it, what constraints it respects, what it can be trusted to do, and what new scientific conclusion becomes possible because it exists.

That is the standard this publication will use: not whether a new model is impressive, but whether it changes how we understand, simulate, observe, or predict the climate system—and whether the evidence supports that change.
